paper_title: JFinBench: A Continuously Refreshable Japanese Financial Benchmark from the Latest Certification Exams

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to finance, creating a need for benchmarks that evaluate their capabilities across financial systems with different regulations and practices. However, existing financial benchmarks provide limited coverage of country-specific financial systems, and they are difficult to keep up to date as released questions leak into training data. We introduce JFinBench, a Japanese financial benchmark comprising 321 examples from the 2026 editions of six regularly administered certification exams covering accounting, tax, financial planning, and banking. To construct it, we develop a human-in-the-loop agentic pipeline in which a coding agent writes exam-specific conversion code and a review page, while a human verifies every example and feeds corrections back to the agent. This pipeline adapts to heterogeneous exam formats and reduces the effort of incorporating new exam editions, enabling periodic refreshes that mitigate data contamination. Evaluating 12 recent LLMs, we find that Claude Fable 5 and GPT-6 Astra exceed 93% overall, while even the best open-weight model, Kimi K3.1 Pro, trails Claude Fable 5 by 12 percentage points. When models can additionally use a terminal and web access, they retrieve the knowledge they lack and every model improves. The gap narrows but about 4 points remain, and the ranking of models stays largely the same, suggesting that knowledge held in the model itself remains valuable even with tools. We release the dataset, the evaluation code, and the construction pipeline.

Code: github.com/SakanaAI/JFinBench Data: huggingface.co/datasets/SakanaAI/JFinBench Figure 1 Human-in-the-loop agentic construction pipeline of JFinBench. Generic scripts transcribe each exam PDF into layout-preserving markdown with VLM, code written by coding agent for each exam turns the transcripts into structured examples, and human verifies every example side by side against the source page and reports problems back to the agent, which fixes its code. 1. Introduction Large language models (LLMs) increasingly take on professional work (Massenkoff & McCrory, 2026), including software engineering (Jimenez et al., 2024), web browsing (Wei et al., 2025), enterprise workflows (Opsahl-Ong et al., 2026; Shepard & Salimans, 2026), economically valuable JFinBench: Continuously Refreshable Japanese Financial Benchmark from the Latest Certification Exams occupational tasks (Patwardhan et al., 2026), and even running business (Backlund & Petersson, 2025; Sugiura et al., 2026a). Finance is critical domain for LLM applications (Zhang et al., 2026), spanning everyday tasks such as answering tax and investment questions as well as more complex tasks requiring specialized financial knowledge (Bigeard et al., 2025; Sugiura et al., 2026b). Accurately assessing these capabilities is essential for advancing the application of LLMs in finance. However, existing financial benchmarks have two important limitations. First, they provide limited coverage of country-specific financial knowledge. Financial expertise depends on local tax rules, accounting standards, and regulations, yet most existing benchmarks (Shah et al., 2022; Xie et al., 2024) focus on English-language data and U.S.-centric settings. For Japanese finance, Hirano (2024) built benchmark from certification exams, but it covers four exams with multiple-choice questions only, leaving free-form answers such as tax calculations and essays, as well as questions that depend on figures, unevaluated. Second, existing benchmarks are difficult to keep up to date. Tax rules and regulations are revised frequently, so questions from past exam editions may test rules that no longer apply. Moreover, once released, benchmark questions can leak into model training data, so evaluation scores may increasingly reflect memorization rather than generalization (Sainz et al., 2023). Although regularly incorporating newly released material can mitigate these issues (He et al., 2026; Jain et al., 2025; White et al., 2025), converting new source documents into reliable structured examples suitable for model evaluation requires substantial effort, hindering frequent updates. We introduce JFinBench, Japanese financial benchmark comprising 321 examples from the 2026 editions of six financial certification exams. These exams cover diverse areas of Japanese finance and its regulations, from accounting and auditing to tax law, financial planning, and banking. They are also administered regularly, so each new edition supplies fresh expert-written questions that postdate the training data of existing models. To convert the exam PDFs into structured examples suitable for model evaluation, we develop the human-in-the-loop agentic pipeline shown in Figure 1. In this pipeline, coding agent generates exam-specific conversion code and review page, while human verifies every example and feeds corrections back to the agent. Because the agent tailors the code to each exam, the pipeline adapts to diverse question formats, including multiple choice, essays, and image-based questions. This reduces the effort required to incorporate new exam editions, making it practical to refresh the benchmark over time. Evaluating 12 recent LLMs, we find that Claude Fable 5 and GPT-6 Astra exceed 93% overall and approach saturation on several exams. In contrast, the best open-weight model, Kimi K3.1 Pro, trails Claude Fable 5 by 12 percentage points, suggesting substantial room for improvement in openweight models specialized Japanese financial capabilities. This gap stands in contrast to agentic coding, where Kimi K3.1 Pro is reported to outperform GPT-6 Astra on Terminal-Bench (Merrill et al., 2026; Moonshot AI, 2026b), suggesting that open-weight models have nearly caught up in domains that model developers prioritize but not in specialized domains such as Japanese finance. Our failure analysis indicates that most errors arise from missing knowledge, while calculation errors are rare. With terminal and web access, most models improve by retrieving missing knowledge from the web. The gap narrows but approximately 4 percentage points remain, and the ranking of models changes little (Spearman 𝜌 = 0.87), suggesting that knowledge held in the models parameters remains valuable even with tools. 2. Related Work Financial benchmarks. Financial benchmarks for LLMs have progressed from relatively simple tasks, such as numerical reasoning over corporate filings in FinQA (Chen et al., 2021), toward more practical and complex ones. The Finance Agent Benchmark has agents research recent SEC filings with web search and EDGAR access (Bigeard et al., 2025), and FrontierFinance evaluates the full 2 JFinBench: Continuously Refreshable Japanese Financial Benchmark from the Latest Certification Exams

These resources primarily focus on English-language financial data and U.S.-centric settings, leaving country-specific financial systems less well covered. For Japanese finance, where LLM applications are an active area of study (Nakagawa et al., 2025; Sugiura et al., 2026b), few benchmarks have begun to address this gap by drawing on certification exams. Masuda et al. (2023) evaluated ChatGPT on the auditing section of the CPA short-answer exam, and Hirano (2024) pioneered benchmark construction from Japanese financial certification exams, covering four exams. JFinBench extends this line of work in three directions. First, it draws on the newest exam editions, held in 2026, to limit contamination, whereas prior benchmarks use editions from 20132023 and undated sample questions. Second, it covers question formats beyond multiple choice, including image-dependent and free-form questions. Third, it comes with pipeline that keeps the benchmark refreshable as new editions are released. Table 1 summarizes the comparison. Exam-based benchmarks. Examinations provide natural source of evaluation data because they are authored by domain experts and designed to distinguish different levels of human competence: MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021) draws on school-level examinations and standardized admission tests. More recent studies have turned to professional licensing examinations, including the bar exam (Choi et al., 2022; Iu & Wong, 2023; Katz et al., 2024; OpenAI, 2024a) and medical licensing exams (Kasai et al., 2023; Nori et al., 2023; Xun et al., 2026), and the mathematics competition AIME (Mathematical Association of America, 2026) has become standard benchmark for reasoning models. JFinBench follows this line of work by using Japanese financial certification exams as source of expert-authored evaluation material. Live benchmarks. persistent challenge for benchmark-based evaluation is data contamination: benchmark questions may enter model training data, so scores come to reflect memorization rather than generalization (Sainz et al., 2023). Post-hoc detection methods exist (Deng et al., 2024; Oren et al., 2024), but more fundamental remedy is to evaluate on material that postdates the training data, as in live benchmarks such as LiveCodeBench, which periodically incorporate newly released problems (He et al., 2026; Jain et al., 2025; White et al., 2025). JFinBench brings this live-benchmark approach to Japanese finance, using the certification exams, which are held regularly and published officially, as recurring source of fresh, expert-authored evaluation material. Scalable benchmark construction. Building benchmark by hand is laborious (Merrill et al., 2026), so growing line of work uses programs and agents to make its construction more efficient and scalable. One approach mines existing artifacts and converts them automatically: SWE-bench (Jimenez et al., 2024) builds tasks from real GitHub issues and the pull requests that resolved them, and ProgramBench (Yang et al., 2026) uses existing programs as references and generates behavioral tests by agent-driven fuzzing. Agents increasingly author the questions as well: OfficeQA Pro V2 (Databricks, 2026) generates them with synthesis, solver, and verification agents and keeps humans 3 JFinBench: Continuously Refreshable Japanese Financial Benchmark from the Latest Certification Exams Exam Exam date Sections Question type MCQ Short Form Essay Examples w/ image CPA short-answer exam Certified Public Tax Accountant FP Level 1, written Financial counter services Level 1 May 2026 Nissho Bookkeeping Level 1 Zensho Bookkeeping Level 1 May 24, 2026 Aug 46, 2026 May 24, 2026 Jun 14, 2026 Jun 28, Total 4 11 2 2 4 2 25 93 50 50 193 15 16 23 87 17 1 18 23 23 93 40 65 66 24 1 6 5 321 12 Table 2 Statistics of JFinBench. The w/ image column counts examples whose question includes an image. Administered by computer-based testing (CBT) without fixed exam day. JFinBench likewise builds on existing artifacts, namely the official exam PDFs, and makes their conversion scalable with human-in-the-loop agentic pipeline, in which coding agent automates most of the work and human verifies the results. 3. JFinBench JFinBench is benchmark of Japanese financial capabilities comprising 321 examples drawn from six certification exams held between May and August 2026, as summarized in Table 2. 3.1. Source exams We select exams that cover core area of Japanese financial practice, whose questions are published as official PDFs by the administering organization with publicly available answer keys, and whose most recent edition was held in 2026. When an exam is offered at multiple levels, we use the highest, Level 1. Below, we give an overview of each of the six exams.1 CPA short-answer exam. The first-stage screening exam of Japans national CPA qualification, administered by the Certified Public Accountants and Auditing Oversight Board under the Financial Services Agency. The exam consists of four subjects, namely financial accounting, management accounting, auditing, and corporate law, all answered as multiple-choice questions (MCQs). Certified Public Tax Accountant exam. The national licensing exam for tax practitioners, administered by the National Tax Council under the National Tax Agency. The exam consists of 11 subjects, two in accounting and nine in tax law, all answered as essays or long-form calculations. FP skill test. The national certification for financial planners at the practitioner level, consisting of written test and practical test. We include the written test. It comprises basic part, which asks knowledge MCQs on topics such as pensions, insurance, tax planning, and inheritance, and an applied part, which poses client scenarios whose answers, such as pension benefits or inheritance-tax amounts for given household, must be computed. Financial counter services skill test. The national certification for bank-counter professionals, combining knowledge MCQs with counter consultations answered as MCQs and short responses. 1The official Japanese names and licenses of the selected exams are given in Appendix A.1. 4 JFinBench: Continuously Refreshable Japanese Financial Benchmark from the Latest Certification Exams Japans de facto standard bookkeeping certification. Level 1 covers advanced Nissho Bookkeeping. financial and cost accounting, such as consolidated statements and standard costing, answered mostly as short computed values, with one full answer form. Zensho Bookkeeping. bookkeeping test administered by the National Association of Commercial High Schools and taken mainly by commercial high school students, covering financial and cost accounting answered mostly as short computed values. 3.2. Construction pipeline The exam PDFs differ in layout across exams and often across questions within an exam, and their tables, answer forms, and figures do not survive standard text extraction tools such as PyMuPDF (PyMuPDF, 2015). We therefore build JFinBench with the human-in-the-loop agentic pipeline shown in Figure 1, which converts the PDFs into structured, machine-readable examples in three steps: generic scripts shared by all exams transcribe the pages, coding agent writes exam-specific code that turns the transcripts into examples, and human verifies every example and feeds corrections back to the agent. We describe each step below. Generic transcription. Shared scripts render each page as an image at 300 dpi and transcribe it into markdown with VLM, Gemini 3.8 Flash (Google, 2026), which preserves the page layout: tables become markdown tables, and figures that cannot be transcribed as text are replaced by explicit placeholders rather than silently dropped. Each transcript is compared with the PyMuPDF-extracted text as character multisets, flagging omissions and hallucinations for inspection. Exam-specific conversion by coding agent. For each exam, coding agent, Claude Code (Anthropic, 2025), writes the code that splits the transcripts into typed example records, attaches options and answer keys, crops figure regions for visual examples, removes non-content artifacts such as page headers and preparatory schools predicted point allocations, and generates side-by-side review page, shown in Appendix A.3. The agent works from natural-language instructions that specify the source URLs and the statutory basis date, so adding an exam requires no manual programming. Human verification and feedback. For every example, one of the authors, native Japanese speaker, compares the final record against the source page on this review page. The reviewer reports problems in natural language, ranging from misparsed options and leftover pagination notes to missing reference material and unclear answer formats, and the agent fixes its code or the records and regenerates the affected examples for re-verification. All 321 examples were verified this way, which took roughly two hours per exam, or about 12 hours in total. The six exams differ widely in format, from multiple choice to blank-filling bookkeeping forms and tax essays across 11 subjects, yet share the same generic scripts, so adding new exam or edition requires only new agent-written code and human verification. Since neither the generic scripts nor the agent-driven workflow is specific to finance, the same pipeline could be applied to other certification exams, such as the national medical licensing or bar exams. 3.3. Statistics and question types Table 2 breaks the 321 examples down by exam and question type. JFinBench has four question types, each with its own grading method described in Section 4.3. MCQ examples are answered by selecting an option. Short answer examples ask for term or an amount written directly. Form examples require structured answer form with up to dozens of interdependent blanks, graded blank by blank. Essay examples ask for long-form theory answer, graded with rubric derived from the answer key. The 321 examples, each separately graded unit, derive from 267 source problems. Multiple choice accounts for 193 examples. The remaining 128 require generated answers, from one-line values to 5 JFinBench: Continuously Refreshable Japanese Financial Benchmark from the Latest Certification Exams full essays. Twelve examples additionally include images, such as land-plot diagrams, served to the models as visual inputs. Representative examples are shown in Appendix A.2. 4. Experimental Setup We evaluate models primarily without tools, answering each example in single API call, so that scores reflect the knowledge stored in the models parameters and its reasoning. Section 5.5 additionally evaluates setting with tools, where models can use terminal and web access to run computations and retrieve knowledge they lack. 4.1. Models We evaluate 12 models: Claude Fable 5 (Anthropic, 2026a), GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI, 2026a), and Gemini 3.8 Flash (Google, 2026) as proprietary models, and Kimi K3.1 Pro, K3, and K2.6 (Kimi Team, 2026; Moonshot AI, 2026a,b), DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (DeepSeek-AI, 2026a,b), Qwen3.8 Flash (Qwen, 2026), MiMo-V2.6-Pro and MiMo-V2.6-Flash (Xiaomi MiMo, 2026), GLM 5.3 Flash (GLM-5 Team, 2026), and Mistral Large 4 (Mistral AI, 2026) as open-weight models. All models accept image inputs. Gemini 3.8 Flash is accessed through Googles official API. All other models are accessed through the OpenRouter API,2 pinned to the model developers official provider, except for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, which is served by DeepInfra. Release dates and reported knowledge cutoffs are listed in Appendix B.1, and every exam postdates every reported cutoff. 4.2. Inference settings We use the developers recommended sampling parameters where published. We set the maximum output length to 131,072 tokens. For each model, we run the maximum and the minimum reasoning effort it supports. Models without an effective effort control use single setting with thinking enabled. Because neither model outputs nor judge decisions are deterministic, every combination of model and effort level is run three times, and we report the mean. 4.3. Scoring Each example is scored by method matched to its question type. MCQ: regex-based answer extraction, with an LLM-judge fallback (Zheng et al., 2023) for malformed outputs. Short answer: an equivalence judge that accepts mathematically or legally equivalent phrasings. Form: blank-level partial credit, i.e., the fraction of blanks matching the answer key, with up to about 40 blanks per form. Essay: rubric-based grading, where the key points of the answer key serve as the rubric and the score is the fraction of key points the response covers. All judges use the same grader model, GPT-5.1 (OpenAI, 2025). The full judge prompts are in Appendix B.4, and the sensitivity of scores to the judge model is analyzed in Appendix B.5, where re-grading with second judge, Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic, 2026b), yields closely matching scores. An exams score is the mean over its examples, and the overall score is the mean over the six exams with equal weight. Cost is computed from measured input/output tokens at the official list prices given in Appendix B.2 and excludes the grader. 4.4. Main results Table 3 reports the main results without tools at maximum reasoning effort. Claude Fable 5 and GPT-6 Astra achieve the highest overall scores of 95.8 and 93.6. The two leaders score 96100 on every exam except the tax accountant exam, where the best score is 79.4. The three proprietary models occupy the top three ranks. The strongest open-weight model, Kimi K3.1 Pro, reaches an overall score of 83.4, full 12 percentage points behind Claude Fable 5, and every open-weight model scores below every proprietary one. This gap contrasts with agentic coding, capability that model developers actively prioritize, where Kimi K3.1 Pro is reported to score 65.7% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, above GPT-6 Astras 58.2% (Moonshot AI, 2026b). On JFinBench, GPT-6 Astra instead leads Kimi K3.1 Pro by 10.2 points. This clear separation suggests that open-weight models lack much of the specialized knowledge of Japanese finance that proprietary models have acquired. 5.2. Performance vs. cost Reasoning models (Guo et al., 2025; OpenAI, 2024b) expose settings, such as reasoning effort, that control how much test-time compute they spend, so models should also be compared on the cost at which they reach given score (Brown, 2026). Evaluation with tools Results without tools measure parametric knowledge and in-context reasoning, but real financial work increasingly involves tools (Bigeard et al., 2025). We therefore also evaluate every model in setting with tools, where for each question the model can use terminal and web access over multiple turns before answering. We run this evaluation with Harbor (Shi et al., 2026), framework for agentic evaluation that runs each task in an isolated container. Each model is evaluated with Harbors Terminus-2 agent harness, with mini-SWE-agent (Yang et al., 2024), and with the developers official harness where one exists, and we report the score of its best harness. Because the web may contain the published answers, the instructions prohibit consulting answer keys, and we audit every trajectory with an LLM. Attempts that used answer material, 8 of the 11,556 with Terminus-2 (0.07%), score 0 (Appendix D.1). Appendix describes the setup in detail and reports further analyses. Tools raise every model. Table 4 compares the two settings. Tool access raises the score of every model, and most for GLM 5.3 Flash, which gains 29.9 points. Taking each models best harness, the gap between the best open-weight and the best proprietary model narrows from 12.4 to 4.4 points, with Kimi K3.1 Pro reaching 92.9 with Kimi Code against GPT-6 Astras 97.3 with Terminus2. Yet tools do not erase the differences between models. The ranking changes little between the two settings (Spearman 𝜌 = 0.87 over the 12 models), and the same three models lead in both. The main exception is GLM 5.3 Flash, which rises from 11th to 7th. Models that know more without tools thus also score higher with them, suggesting that knowledge stored in the parameters helps an agent decide what to look up and how to apply what it finds. Retrieval complements rather than replaces this knowledge, so JFinBench remains informative when models can use tools. Appendix D.3 compares the harnesses in detail. How agents use tools. To see how the models improve with tools, we analyze which kinds of tools the agents use in the first run, where an attempt is one agent session on one question. GPT-6 Luna (OpenAI, 2026b) reads all commands of each attempt and labels whether it involves file operation, web retrieval, calculation, or other commands. Figure 5 shows, for two proprietary and two openweight models with Terminus-2, the one harness common to all models, the share of the 321 tasks in which the agent uses each kind of tool. Every model operates on files in almost every task, which is expected because the final answer must be written to file. Web retrieval occurs in 56 to 66% of the tasks, as the agents look up knowledge they lack. Calculation occurs in 9 to 28% of the tasks, where the agents compute amounts such as taxes, depreciation, and present values with Python or bc. Agents consult the statutes. Figure 6 shows the share of tasks in which the agent accesses each of the most frequent domains. All four models most often consult e-Gov, the governments statute database,3 and the open-weight models also query search engines far more often, for example DuckDuckGo in 47% of the tasks for GLM 5.3 Flash against at most 11% for the proprietary models. 3https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/ 10 JFinBench: Continuously Refreshable Japanese Financial Benchmark from the Latest Certification Exams Figure 12 in Appendix D.4 shows trajectory in which the agent retrieves the statutes in force on the exams basis date from e-Gov and answers question it fails without tools. These results suggest that, with tools, models raise their scores mainly by supplementing missing knowledge and, on computation questions, by calculating exactly. 6. Conclusion We introduced JFinBench, Japanese financial benchmark built from the 2026 editions of six certification exams with human-in-the-loop agentic pipeline that reduces the human effort of future updates. The leading proprietary models are near the ceiling except on tax practice, while the best open-weight model trails the best proprietary model by 12 points. Missing knowledge is the main challenge. Tool use helps substantially, raising every model and narrowing but not closing the gap between the best proprietary and best open-weight models, from 12 to about 4 points, while the ranking of models stays largely the same. We hope JFinBench encourages progress in domains that general benchmarks overlook. Limitations Coverage. We include only exams whose questions are published as PDFs by the administering organization. Exams that do not publish past questions as official PDFs, such as the Securities Analyst (CMA) exam,4 are out of scope. Contamination. Every exam postdates every reported knowledge cutoff listed in Appendix B.1, but this temporal separation does not guarantee the absence of contamination. Most vendors do not report cutoff at all, and reported cutoffs are self-declared, vary in definition across developers, and may differ from the effective cutoff of the training data (Cheng et al., 2024). Models may also be post-trained on data collected after the stated date. Refreshing the benchmark with future exam editions remains the primary mitigation. Saturation. The two leading proprietary models already score 96100 on every exam except the tax accountant exam, so JFinBench offers limited headroom for differentiating them. The benchmark remains well suited to tracking the progress of open-weight models, which still trail by 12 percentage points. For frontier models, promising directions include filtering future editions to the hardest questions, as in Humanitys Last Exam (Phan et al., 2026), commissioning new expert-authored questions (Merrill et al., 2026), and building agentic financial benchmarks (Bigeard et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026). Ethical Considerations The exam material contains no personal data, as persons appearing in problem statements are fictitious. high JFinBench score does not constitute professional qualification, and our results should not be read as evidence that current models can substitute for licensed tax accountants or CPAs. Because JFinBench is built from officially published examinations, we see little risk of social harm or misuse arising from the benchmark itself. Each attempt has wall-clock budget of six hours. Figure input. Terminus-2 passes only text to the model, so for the figure-dependent examples we add view_image command to the container. When the agent runs it on an image file, the harness attaches the image to the next observation, so the agent can view any image, as the official harnesses do with their own file-reading tools. The figure is placed in directory the agent can access, and the instruction states where it is and how to view it. In addition to prohibiting answer keys and prep-school solutions in Detecting answer-key use. the task instructions, we audit every trajectory with GPT-6 Luna (OpenAI, 2026b), covering all 11,556 Terminus-2 attempts and the 24,196 attempts of the harness comparison. Luna receives condensed trajectory, consisting of each command (first 2,000 characters) and each tool output (first 1,500 and last 500 characters), and is asked whether the agent opened this exams answers, answer bulletins, model answers, or past-exam explanations, whether such an answer appeared in search snippet that the final answer follows, and whether the agent tampered with grading. Attempts that opened such material, or whose final answer matches an answer shown in searchresult snippet, score 0, regardless of the agents intent. Without them, neither the heirs nor the land values can be determined. While looking for way to read the figures, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 found the key and made eight API calls to Gemini 2.5 Flash and Pro, having them transcribe as text the formulas that the National Tax Agency publishes only as images and the pages of the question PDF, including the land diagrams, that it downloaded itself. These actions are therefore strategies that the models devised on their own to complete the task when the image was unavailable, and they may not amount to cheating. Still, these cases are an intriguing illustration of how readily LLM agents exploit resources found in their environment to accomplish given task. PostTrainBench (Rank et al., 2026) likewise reports agents using API keys they found to generate synthetic data without authorization. (c) Type-2 interim consolidated statements must include the statement of changes in equity and the cash flow statement.
